title: How much does a business website cost? What affects the price and how to avoid hidden costs
excerpt: What affects the price of a business website, which costs come after launch and how to avoid hidden costs. A practical guide before you ask for a quote.
content:
In short: nobody can give you a fair price for a business website off the top of their head, because it depends on a few concrete things — how many pages and services you have, whether the design is built from scratch, who writes the copy and which extra features you need. The good news is that you can know exactly what you are paying for before any work starts. Below we show you what to look at so there are no surprises.

Why there is no single price for a business website

A business website for an electrician who works alone and one for a clinic with ten services and three doctors are two very different things, even though both are called a “business website”. The number of pages, the amount of text, the photos, the forms and how much the site needs to show up on Google all differ.

That is why a serious web design company first asks you a few questions and only then gives you a price. If you get a figure before anyone has asked what you do and what you want from the site, that price is either too high or leaves out things you will end up paying for later.

What affects the price of a business website

1. How many pages and services you have

Every important service deserves its own page or section, because that is how you show up for specific searches on Google, not just for your company name. The more services and pages you have, the more design, structure and copywriting work is involved.

2. Custom design or a template

A carefully adapted template can be a very good choice for a business that is just starting out. A design built from scratch costs more, but it looks exactly like your brand and is built around what you want visitors to do: call, ask for a quote or book an appointment.

3. Who writes the copy and where the photos come from

Copy is often what holds a website back. If you write it yourself, the price goes down. If we write it, you also pay for the writing, but you get text designed for customers and for Google. The same goes for photos: real photos of your business convert far better than stock images.

4. Extra features

A simple contact form is almost always included. The price goes up when you need things like:

  • online bookings, with a calendar and notifications;
  • a website in several languages;
  • a blog or news section you can update yourself;
  • a connection to other software — invoicing, a CRM or a booking system.

5. Basic SEO and speed

A website that does not show up on Google is like a business card kept in a drawer. A sound page structure, titles, descriptions, loading speed and a link to your Google Business Profile make the difference between a site that brings in customers and one that simply exists.

The costs that come after launch

The launch price is not the only cost. Before you sign, ask who pays for what, and how often:

  • Domain renewal — paid every year.
  • Hosting — the server your website lives on.
  • Maintenance — security updates, backups and checking that everything works. See what a monthly maintenance plan includes.
  • Changes — new text, photos, prices or pages added after launch.

There is nothing wrong with these costs, as long as you know about them from the start. The problem is finding out only once the website is finished.

How to avoid hidden costs

  • Ask for a written quote listing everything included: number of pages, copy, photos, forms, basic SEO, domain and hosting.
  • Ask for a fixed price, agreed before work begins, not an hourly rate.
  • Ask whose name the domain is registered in and whether the website is fully yours once it is paid for.
  • Find out how changes after launch are charged.
  • Check the portfolio: real websites, delivered to real clients, that you can open yourself.

What to prepare to get an accurate quote

The more we know at the start, the more accurate the quote. If you can, prepare:

  • a list of the services or products you want to present;
  • 2–3 websites you like (even from another industry) and what you like about them;
  • your logo and colours, if you have them;
  • what you want visitors to do: call, ask for a quote, book an appointment;
  • whether you already have copy and photos or need us to create them.

How we work

At C Design, we set the price of a business website after a short, free call and put it in the quote before we start — a fixed price with no hidden costs. The .ro domain and hosting are included, and the website belongs to you. See what a business website from us includes and the projects we have delivered. If you are just starting a business, the Online start-up package also includes your logo and social media accounts.

Frequently asked questions

Is a cheap website a bad idea?

Not necessarily. A simple, well-made website can bring in customers very well. The problem starts when a low price comes with gaps: no basic SEO, hard to use on a phone, or a domain registered in someone else’s name. Compare what is included, not just the figure.

Can I start with a small website and expand it later?

Yes, and it is often the best option. You start with the essential pages, see what brings in customers and add pages or features along the way. What matters is that the website is built so it can grow.

How quickly do I get a quote?

After a short call in which you tell us what you do and what you want from the website. If you have the items above ready, the quote is both faster and more accurate.

title: Template or custom design? When each one makes sense
excerpt: When an adapted template is enough and when a custom design is worth it. What makes a quality website, whichever option you choose.
content:
In short: a carefully adapted template is a good choice when you are just starting out and need a clean website quickly. A design built from scratch is worth it when you want to stand out, have a clear brand or need a specific journey for your customers. Below is how to choose, without the jargon.

What “template” and “custom design” actually mean

A template (or theme) is a ready-made design that you adapt: you add your logo, colours, copy and photos. The structure of the pages is largely set in advance.

A custom design starts from your business: who your customers are, what they are looking for and what you want them to do on the site. Only then are the pages designed, the fonts and colours chosen and the information laid out.

Neither is “right” in itself. They are different tools for different situations.

When a template is enough

  • You are just starting a business and want to be online as soon as possible, on a small budget.
  • You have only a few pages: about, services, contact.
  • You do not yet have a defined brand — logo, colours, tone — so there is nothing to “translate” into a unique design.
  • You want to test an idea before investing more.

Even with a template, the adaptation is what makes the difference: copy written for your customers, real photos, the order of the sections and a contact button in the right place. A template left exactly as it came is recognisable straight away.

When a custom design is worth it

  • You are in a crowded market and your website needs to set you apart from competitors using the same themes.
  • You already have a brand and want the website to look exactly like it.
  • You have a specific customer journey: bookings, multi-step quote requests, a customer account, a configurator.
  • The website is your main source of customers, so every detail that increases enquiries matters.

Examples from our portfolio: for APG Garage, a car repair shop, we built a website with online bookings and a customer account. For WSD Logistics, a towing company, the design is built for someone stuck at the roadside with a phone in their hand: the phone number is the first thing you see.

What matters more than the option you choose

Whichever route you take, a quality website has a few things in common:

  • It works really well on a phone. Most visitors will see you there.
  • It loads quickly. A slow website loses visitors before they have read anything.
  • It is clear what to do. One main call to action — call, get a quote, book — visible on every page.
  • The copy talks about the customer, not just the company: what problem you solve and why they should choose you.
  • It is built properly for Google: titles, descriptions, page structure and speed.
  • You can update it without depending on someone else for every comma.

Common mistakes

  • choosing a template packed with animations and effects that slow the site down;
  • keeping the theme’s demo text and photos;
  • paying for a custom design but starting without any copy, so the website sits unfinished for months;
  • judging the design only on a computer, not on a phone.

Can you switch from one to the other later?

Yes. Many businesses start with a simple website and move to a design of their own once they know better what brings in customers. What you can do from the start so you lose nothing: keep the domain in your name, write copy you can reuse and ask for the website to be built properly for Google, so the ranking you earn is not lost in the switch. We wrote more about the right moment in Old website: fix it or rebuild it?

How we work

At C Design we tell you honestly which option suits you after a short, free call. If you are just starting out, the Online start-up package includes the website, the logo and your social media accounts. If you need a website built around your business, see our website design service and our projects.

Frequently asked questions

Does a template-based website rank worse on Google?

Not because of the template. Google looks at content, structure, speed and how useful the website is for visitors. A well-adapted, fast template can rank very well; a heavy one full of effects can rank poorly.

Can I see the design before the website is finished?

Yes. With a custom design you first get the design proposal for the main pages, we discuss it and only then move on to building the website.

Who writes the copy?

You can write it yourself or we can write it, based on what you tell us about your business. Copy written for customers and for Google often makes more difference than the design itself.

Not sure which option suits you? Book a free call and we will tell you honestly, or get a quote straight away.

title: Old website: fix it or rebuild it? Signs it is time for a redesign
excerpt: The signs your website needs a redesign, when a fix is enough and how to change your website without losing the ranking you have earned on Google.
content:
In short: an old website does not need rebuilding just because it is a few years old. It is worth fixing when the problems are small and isolated, and rebuilding when it no longer works well on a phone, is slow, can no longer be updated or has stopped bringing in enquiries. Below are the signs to look for and the steps for changing your website without losing what you have gained on Google.

Signs your website needs a redesign

1. It looks or works badly on a phone

Open your website on a phone and try to do what a customer would: find a service, see how to contact you, send a message. If you have to pinch to zoom, the buttons are too small or the menu will not open, you are losing customers every day.

2. It loads slowly

A slow website is abandoned before it has had a chance to say anything. Slow loading usually comes from unoptimised photos, too many plugins added over time and outdated technology. Sometimes it can be fixed; sometimes it is simpler to start again.

3. You can no longer update it

You have lost the password, the company that built it no longer replies or every small change turns into a project. A website you cannot update ends up with prices, services and photos that no longer match reality.

4. It no longer brings in enquiries

If people tell you they found you on Google but the form on your website receives almost nothing, the problem is usually the site: the message is unclear, the contact button is hard to find or the form is too long.

5. It no longer looks like your business

You have new services, a new logo, different customers from a few years ago. If the website still describes the business you were back then, visitors get the wrong picture of you.

6. Security problems

Browser warnings, no security certificate (the address does not start with “https”), strange pages appearing overnight or an admin system that has not been updated in years. These need fixing immediately, whatever you decide about the design.

When a fix is enough

Not every problem calls for a new website. Often a few targeted changes are enough:

  • optimising the photos and removing plugins that are no longer used;
  • rewriting the copy for customers, with a clear call to action on every page;
  • a shorter contact form and a call button that is visible on phones;
  • updating the system and the security certificate;
  • proper titles and descriptions for Google.

The simple rule: if the structure is good and there are only a few problems, fix it. If the problems are in the foundations — old technology, a site not designed for phones, impossible to update — rebuild it.

How to redesign without losing your Google ranking

An old website often has one valuable thing: pages that Google knows and shows. A careless redesign can lose them. What to watch for:

  • List your existing pages and see which ones bring in visitors.
  • Keep the addresses of important pages or set up permanent (301) redirects from the old addresses to the new ones.
  • Do not throw away good content: rewrite and improve it rather than deleting it.
  • Submit the new sitemap in Google Search Console after launch and watch for errors in the first few weeks.
  • Keep your domain. Changing the domain at the same time as the design makes the switch much riskier.

What to prepare before a redesign

  • what you like and dislike about your current website;
  • what customers ask you most often, by phone or email;
  • the services you want to sell more of now;
  • the login details for your domain, hosting and admin, if you have them;
  • 2–3 websites you like and why.

How we work

At C Design we first look at your current website and tell you honestly whether it is worth fixing or rebuilding. If we rebuild it, we keep what works on Google and redirect the old addresses. See our website design service, our projects and what the maintenance plan includes, so your new website does not age as quickly.

Frequently asked questions

How often should a website be rebuilt?

There is no fixed number of years. A well-built, well-maintained website can last a long time with small updates. You rebuild it when the signs above appear, not by the calendar.

Will I lose customers from Google if I change my website?

No, if the redesign is done carefully: addresses kept or redirected, good content kept and the sitemap submitted in Google Search Console. There may be small fluctuations at first, which usually settle down.

Can I keep the copy and photos from my old website?

Yes. We use what is good and improve the rest. Real photos of your business are often worth more than any new stock image.

Not sure whether your website needs fixing or rebuilding? Book a free call and we will look at it together, or get a quote.

title: How to choose a web design company: 9 questions to ask before you sign
excerpt: The 9 questions to ask a web design company before you sign, the answers to expect and the warning signs that save you from surprises.
content:
In short: you cannot judge a web design company by how good its own website looks, but you can by how it answers a few simple questions. Below are 9 questions to ask before you sign, the answers to expect and the warning signs that should send you looking elsewhere.

Why the choice matters, not just the price

A website is not finished on launch day. You will need changes, updates and someone who picks up the phone when something goes wrong. You are really choosing a partner you will work with for years, not just someone to “make a website”. That is why it pays to ask the questions below from the very first conversation.

9 questions to ask before you sign

1. Can you show me real websites you have built?

Ask for links to websites that are live right now and that you can open on your phone. Check whether they load quickly, whether they are easy to read and whether it is clear what you are supposed to do on them. Screenshots and mock-ups are useful, but a live site tells you much more. All our projects are in our portfolio, with notes on what we aimed for in each one.

2. What questions do you have for me?

It sounds odd, but it is the best test. A serious company wants to know what you do, who your customers are, what you want visitors to do on the site and how people find your business today. If you get a quote without a single question, the website will be built to a formula, not around your business.

3. What exactly is included in the quote?

The number of pages, the copy, the photos, the forms, the mobile version, basic SEO, the domain and hosting. Everything should be in writing. “Complete website” means nothing if you do not know what it contains. We explain what affects the cost in detail in How much does a business website cost?

4. Is the price fixed or hourly?

A fixed price, agreed before work begins, protects you from surprises. Hourly billing can suit large projects that are hard to estimate, but for a business website you should know from the start what you are paying.

5. Whose name is the domain registered in?

The domain should be in your name or your company’s. If it is in the agency’s name and one day you want to leave, you could lose your website address and everything you have built on Google with it.

6. Is the website mine once I have paid for it?

Ask whether you get full access and whether you can move the site to another company if you ever want to. The right answer is “yes”, with no hidden conditions in the contract.

7. What happens after launch?

Who handles security updates, backups and small changes? How quickly does someone respond when you have a problem? Ask from the start how maintenance works and what it covers.

8. How will you help me show up on Google?

A website nobody finds does not bring in customers. The company should explain simply what it does for SEO: page structure, titles, descriptions, speed and the link to your Google Business Profile. Be wary of anyone who promises a “guaranteed first place” — nobody can guarantee that.

9. Who will actually work on my project?

You want to know who you will talk to when you have a question and how you will communicate: phone, email, WhatsApp, online meetings. A single point of contact who knows the project saves you a lot of repeated explanations.

Warning signs

  • you get a price before anyone finds out what you do;
  • the quote has a single line: “business website”;
  • you cannot see a single real website they have built;
  • you are promised first place on Google;
  • the domain stays in the web design company’s name;
  • it is not clear who will help you after launch.

Freelancer or agency?

Both can work. A good freelancer can be an excellent choice for a small project, as long as you have a plan for the times they are not available. An agency usually has several skills under one roof — design, development, copywriting, SEO — and more continuity. What matters is less the format and more the answers to the 9 questions above.

How we work

At C Design we start with a short, free call in which we ask about your business, your customers and what you want from the website. You then get a written quote with a fixed price and everything that is included. The domain is in your name, the website belongs to you and after launch you have a point of contact who knows the project. See what a business website from us looks like.

Frequently asked questions

How many quotes should I ask for?

Two or three are usually enough to compare. More important than the number is comparing quotes on the same criteria: what is included, who owns the domain and what happens after launch.

Does it matter if the company is in my town?

Not necessarily. Most projects work very well online, through video calls and messages. It matters more that they understand your market and your customers. If you would still like a company that knows your area, see our pages for each city.

What documents should I receive?

A written quote listing everything included, a contract or order confirmation and, at the end, the login details for the website, domain and hosting.

Want to put the 9 questions to us? Book a free call or get a quote — we will answer every one, with no obligation.

title: Web design for small businesses: the complete guide
excerpt: Which pages you need, what to put on them, how to get found on Google in your area and which mistakes to avoid. A practical guide with portfolio examples.
content:
In short: for a small business, a good website is not the most complicated one, but the one that quickly answers a customer’s three questions — what you do, why you and how to get in touch. The guide below takes you step by step: which pages you need, what to put on them, how to get found on Google and which mistakes to avoid.

Why a small business needs a website

Facebook and Instagram pages are useful, but they are not yours: the rules change, posts get lost in the feed and people searching on Google struggle to find the important information. A website is your own space, where you control what customers see: your services, opening hours, the area you cover, reviews and a clear contact button. For many small businesses, it is also the first place a new customer decides whether to call you.

Which pages you need

For most small businesses, a few well-made pages are enough:

  • Home page — who you are, what you do, who for, and a clear call to action: call, get a quote, book.
  • Services — ideally a page or section for each important service, so you show up for specific searches.
  • About us — the people behind the business, your experience, real photos.
  • Reviews or projects — proof that others were happy.
  • Contact — phone, email, area covered, opening hours and a short form.

If you sell products at fixed prices, you may need an online shop. If you work by appointment, an online booking system can save you a lot of phone calls.

What makes a small business website bring in customers

A clear message in the first few seconds

Visitors need to understand straight away what you do and where. “Plumbing in Ploiești, same-day call-outs” says much more than “Complete solutions for your home”.

One main call to action

Decide what you want visitors to do and put that button everywhere. For many local businesses, a call button visible on phones brings in the most enquiries.

Real photos

Your workshop, your team, your work, your products. Real photos build trust much faster than stock images the customer has already seen on ten other websites.

Speed and mobile

Most customers will see you on a phone, often in a hurry. The website has to load quickly and be easy to use with one finger.

How to get found on Google in your area

  • Your Google Business Profile (formerly Google My Business), filled in properly and linked to your website.
  • Your town and area in the copy, where it makes sense, not crammed in everywhere.
  • A page for each important service, with its own title and description.
  • Reviews, asked for regularly from happy customers.
  • Identical contact details on your website, on Google and in online directories.

We go into more detail on our SEO and local SEO page.

Examples from our portfolio

A few small businesses we have built websites for, each with different needs:

  • Traditum By Victoria — an artisan cake shop that works to order. The website puts the products front and centre and leads to a quote request, not a shopping basket.
  • APG Garage — a car repair shop in Bucharest, with online bookings and a customer account.
  • Cosmin Tătulescu — a family photographer, with a one-page website and bookings for Christmas photo sessions.
  • WSD Logistics — a towing company, with a website built for someone who needs help right away.

For automotive businesses we also have a dedicated page: web design for car repair shops and automotive businesses.

Common mistakes

  • too much text about the company and too little about what the customer gets;
  • a phone number hidden in the footer;
  • long forms with unnecessary required fields;
  • out-of-date information: opening hours, prices or services that no longer apply;
  • a website launched and then forgotten, with no updates and no backups.

How we work

At C Design we work a lot with small businesses and know that every investment has to make sense. We start with a free call, suggest only the pages you need and send you a written quote with a fixed price, domain and hosting included. If you are just starting out, see the Online start-up package. You will find more about costs in How much does a business website cost? and about choosing a company in How to choose a web design company.

Frequently asked questions

Do I need a website if I already have a Facebook page?

Yes, if you want people to find you on Google and you want control over your information. A Facebook page is useful for community and news; a website is where a new customer decides whether to contact you.

Can I update the website myself?

Yes. We show you how to change the text, photos and basic information. For bigger changes, or if you would rather not deal with it, there is the monthly plan.

What if I do not have any copy or photos?

That is not a problem. We help with the copy, starting from a conversation about your business, and tell you which photos are worth taking. Even a few real photos taken on a phone in good light are better than stock images.

Want a website that brings customers to your business? Get a free quote or book a 30-minute call — no obligation.
